standfirst: Three children raised as siblings by two fathers who were barely coping, filmed with enough restraint that the first six hours are as good as anything 2024 produced. Then the kids grow up and a love triangle gets grafted onto the same people, and the last four hours reach for illness and estrangement instead of finishing the story they started. Everything below holds a made family together without breaking it to fill episodes.

picks.why: One alley, two households, and children who eat at whichever table is closest. Family by Choice runs the same arrangement under one roof: adults who are broke and decent, kids who become siblings by proximity, and a camera that stays at kitchen height. Both are at their best watching a child be fed by someone else's parent. Difference: Reply 1988 keeps its ensemble in balance for the full run, where Family by Choice narrows to a couple and mislays the household it spent six hours building.

Two people with no blood between them who are the only family each other has left. It shares the exact thing that makes the early Family by Choice work: care shown through chores, meals and small acts of custody rather than declarations. Ten episodes, no filler, and every one of them is about somebody being claimed. Difference: there is no romance to protect here, so nothing gets softened to keep a pairing viable.

Parents who quietly ruin themselves so a child gets a shot. Same subject as the fathers in Family by Choice, taken seriously across a whole life instead of used as backstory. If the scene where a broke man pretends he is fine is what got you, this is sixteen episodes of that scene done at full strength. Difference: Tangerines earns its grief over sixty years, while Family by Choice buys it with a late medical thread.

A parent whose love arrives shaped like damage. Both shows are about children carrying the cost of an adult who was doing their best under conditions that made their best cruel, and both are funnier than that sounds for at least half their length. The village comedy sits on top of a real argument about what a parent owes. Difference: this one keeps the parent at the centre and never hands the story over to the grown kids.

Grown children who cannot start anything without their parents' history in the room. The specific awkwardness of dating somebody your mother has known since he was six is the part of Family by Choice that actually lands after the time jump, and Love Next Door is built entirely from it. Warm, low stakes, well cast. Difference: there is no wound at the centre, so it never has to choose between the family and the couple.

The friendship that keeps a wrecked kid upright. It goes at the thing Family by Choice keeps flinching from: a young man whose home life is not survivable and a friend who decides to stay anyway, with no adult arriving to fix it. Twelve episodes, quiet, and honest about how much help costs the person giving it. Difference: no parents, no household, and the ending is harder to sit with.

against.title: Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha
against.why: The default warm pick, and the wrong one. Family by Choice is about children raised by men who could not cope; Cha-Cha-Cha is about a village that has already healed and now enjoys itself. Grief there is a late reveal, not the weather. Watch it if you want comfort, not if you want the thing this show is doing in its first six hours.

against.title: Go Ahead
against.why: The Chinese original, and reaching for it next is a trap. It runs fifty episodes, it does the childhood half better, and it makes the remake look thinner rather than scratching the same itch. Come back to it in a year when the comparison has stopped being annoying.

against.title: Racket Boys
against.why: Paired for the warm teenage ensemble, and the ensemble is genuinely lovely. It is also a sports comedy about kids with functional parents. Nothing in it is trying to survive anything, which is the whole engine of Family by Choice.
